2611.31944.tldr: Training-free KV retrieval for autoregressive video world models: camera-geometry grounding plus low-resolution draft attention selects history blocks, with CPU offload and tile-wise streaming attention. Claims 3.27× speedup and 42.2% less peak memory than offloaded baselines, enabling a 33B model on one H100.
2611.31944.why: Directly relevant to efficient inference for video diffusion transformers and long-horizon 3D-consistent world models, especially memory retrieval and sparse attention over KV history.
2611.31944.reason: Efficient KV-cache retrieval for interactive video world models, directly core interest
2611.31944.qn: Sensible systems design with theory, but gains are over offload baselines and narrow.
2611.31944.abs: Interactive video world models enable action- and camera-controlled exploration, yet struggle to maintain consistent spatial geometry and appearance when revisiting previously explored locations. Historical KV caches help auto-regressive video diffusion models maintain long-term consistency, but their retrieval and attention computation introduce substantial latency as history grows. We propose DraftKV, a training-free framework that retrieves historical KV caches based on geometric grounding and query-conditioned relevance, while combining CPU offloading with tile-wise streaming attention to reduce GPU memory usage and inference latency. Theoretically, we show that draft relevance reproduces the mean branch of full-resolution block relevance exactly, so its deviation is confined to the $\beta$-weighted max branch, and we bound retrieval utility loss in terms of the measured Top-K selection overlap. We further show that draft relevance cannot distinguish blocks with similar pooled descriptors regardless of camera pose, motivating geometric grounding before refinement. Then, we introduce streaming CG-Attention, which overlaps CPU-to-GPU KV transfers with attention computation through tile-wise streaming, hiding transfer latency while maintaining bounded GPU memory usage. Experiments across diverse model families show that DraftKV achieves superior generation quality and consistency while achieving $3.27\times$ end-to-end speedup and 42.2% peak GPU memory reduction over other CPU-offloaded KV cache retrieval methods. Notably, DraftKV enables high-quality interactive world generation with historical KV retrieval on a single H100 GPU using SolarWM-33B.

2611.32445.tldr: M2R is a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own attention features on mesh surfaces (in each object's frame) and retrieves them by rasterization, giving persistent appearance for moving objects and multiple agents at 40 FPS at 720p.
2611.32445.why: Directly relevant to video world models with 3D consistency and efficient few-step causal inference; mesh-indexed KV memory is an interesting alternative to frame-based or pose-based memory.
2611.32445.reason: Mesh-anchored persistent appearance for interactive video world models; core fit
2611.32445.qn: Clever surface-indexed KV memory with strong claimed gains; synthetic-trained, evidence only partly visible.
2611.32445.abs: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

2611.32035.tldr: Training-free FP4 attention for video DiTs: compensates Q/K rounding error along top per-head eigen-directions appended as extra channels, plus softmax kernel optimizations. Wan2.2 attention is 2.13-2.82x faster than BF16, and end-to-end 1.55-1.80x faster, with lower LPIPS than prior 4-bit kernels.
2611.32035.why: Directly targets efficient video DiT inference through low-precision and sparse-style attention kernels, with real speedups on Blackwell and Rubin GPUs, useful if you deploy Wan-style video models.
2611.32035.reason: Training-free low-precision attention for video diffusion transformers, directly on core efficiency interest
2611.32035.qn: Sound error analysis and real kernels; evaluated on LPIPS and limited hardware.
2611.32035.abs: Self-attention over tens of thousands of tokens dominates the generation time of video diffusion transformers, because its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. The FP4 matrix products of modern GPUs can speed up attention, but the 4-bit rounding of the queries Q and the keys K introduces large errors. We show that the exponential in softmax amplifies the error of their product QK, which therefore dominates the attention error. We propose DeCo-Attention, a co-design of algorithm and system for low-precision attention. DeCo-Attention is training-free and compensates the rounding error of Q and K along a few principal directions found by a per-head eigendecomposition. The lightweight compensation terms are appended to Q and K as extra channels, so the FP4 matrix product corrects its own rounding error while it computes the attention scores. Once the products run in FP4, the softmax bounds the kernel, and we optimize the softmax so that the gain of FP4 computation translates into realized speedup. With QK in FP4, we implement DeCo-Attention with the rest of attention in FP8 on GB300 and VR200 and in FP4 on RTX PRO 6000. On Wan2.2, these kernels run 2.13x, 2.49x, and 2.82x faster than BF16 attention, and the whole generation runs 1.55x, 1.68x, and 1.80x faster. On four video generation models, the FP8 configuration achieves LPIPS comparable to prior 8-bit QK methods, and the fully FP4 configuration lower LPIPS than prior fully 4-bit kernels.

2611.32198.tldr: MoGe-4D is a feed-forward model that predicts paired allocentric/egocentric dynamic point maps for source-target frame queries, using a cached context encoder plus a lightweight query decoder. It reports 28–44% lower tracking error and faster inference, and a rigid-body-compressed synthetic dataset (RigIDTrack).
2611.32198.why: It directly addresses feed-forward 4D reconstruction and tracking with efficient dense querying (caching, decoupled resolution), building on MoGe and D4RT-style world-model foundations.
2611.32198.reason: Feed-forward dense 4D reconstruction and tracking; squarely on core topic
2611.32198.qn: Strong unified design and efficiency gains; introduction-level evidence only, benchmarks not yet verified.
2611.32198.abs: Reconstructing dynamic scenes from RGB video requires reasoning about both 3D geometry and motion across viewpoints, yet existing methods either split reconstruction and tracking into fragmented pipelines or face prohibitive dense spatiotemporal decoding costs. We introduce MoGe-4D, a feed-forward framework that unifies geometry and motion prediction via ordered queries of paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps. Each query maps source pixels to a target time simultaneously in both camera frames, resolving relative camera pose in closed form while flexibly serving depth, dynamic registration, and dense 3D tracking. For efficient dense querying, MoGe-4D decouples scene modeling from query decoding: a high-capacity context encoder caches coarse global spatiotemporal features once, while a lightweight query encoder rapidly decodes dense point maps at flexible resolutions. Furthermore, as supervising dense 4D queries demands continuous 3D correspondences whose raw trajectory storage is prohibitive, we introduce RigIDTrack, a synthetic data pipeline and dataset that compresses surface dynamics into rigidity-regularized affine bodies, recovering exact arbitrary-frame 3D trajectories with $\sim15\%$ storage overhead over RGB-D video. Across diverse benchmarks, MoGe-4D achieves state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, matches dedicated 3D foundation models in reconstruction, and runs substantially faster than prior 4D baselines.

2611.31428.tldr: Fuses sparse-view 3DGS renders with a feed-forward NVS prior using a one-parameter first-order low-pass filter (prior for low frequencies, Gaussians for high), then distills fused images into the Gaussians; gains 1.0–1.2 dB on LLFF and Mip-NeRF 360.
2611.31428.why: Directly relevant to sparse-view 3DGS and feed-forward reconstruction priors; the frequency-domain complementarity and distillation into fast Gaussians is a reusable recipe.
2611.31428.reason: Sparse-view 3DGS enhanced by feed-forward priors with real-time rendering
2611.31428.qn: Simple, well-motivated frequency analysis; gains moderate, limited to sparse-view benchmarks.
2611.31428.abs: Gaussian splatting from sparse training views renders high-quality images near training views, but reconstruction quality degrades at distant regions, which are undersampled by the training set. Feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) models use strong learned priors to resample the scene from substantially different viewpoints, but they take more than ten times as long to render and produce high-frequency artifacts on out-of-domain scenes. We propose a plug-and-play method that enhances an existing sparse-view Gaussian model with a pretrained feed-forward NVS model. We observe that the two are complementary in the frequency domain: the prior is more accurate at low frequencies, and the Gaussians at high frequencies. The reliability of the prior relative to the Gaussians is inversely proportional to the image frequency, so the optimal fusion weight is a first-order low-pass filter with one parameter that can be fitted. Our key idea is then to intelligently fuse the reliable part of each of the two methods. To remove the slow feed-forward model at render time, we use these fused images as teachers and distill them back into Gaussians, balanced with supervision from input views. Our method improves the quality of various sparse-view Gaussian methods without sacrificing rendering speed, and our analysis works on different prior models. Project page: https://linwk20.github.io/spectral-fusion-gs/

2611.32562.tldr: Sol³ is a training-free hierarchical sparse attention method for video diffusion. It routes blocks to Full or Mixed, then selects tokens in Mixed blocks for exact computation and approximates the rest with representatives. It reports 86% sparsity and 3.07× attention speedup.
2611.32562.why: Directly relevant to efficient inference for video diffusion transformers via training-free sparse attention, including world simulation tasks. It is a possible drop-in baseline for acceleration.
2611.32562.reason: Training-free hierarchical sparse attention for video diffusion acceleration, a core interest
2611.32562.qn: Incremental refinement of Sol-Attn; evidence is unverified from the intro alone.
2611.32562.abs: Sol-Attn (Sparsifying online attention) combines sparse exact computation with low-cost representative approximation to accelerate training-free inference in diffusion video models. However, intra-block attention can focus on only a few tokens. While preserving these key interactions exactly, the block-level decision incurs the cost of evaluating many low-response members. We propose Sol$^{3}$, a training-free hierarchical sparse attention method that further refines how exact computations are allocated. First, we introduce Gaussian-guided hierarchical routing, which determines the scope of exact computation step by step, from blocks to tokens, using statistical thresholds at each level. Only a subset of members within Mixed blocks that require refinement is selected for exact computation, while representative terms approximate the remaining members. We further design heterogeneous routing statistics that combine block-center correlations with variations in Key and Value within blocks to identify blocks that are difficult to approximate. Among these Mixed blocks, we uniformly compare raw token relevance to select members requiring exact computation. Experiments on video generation, audio-video co-generation, and world simulation tasks demonstrate that Sol$^{3}$ achieves 86% attention sparsity and delivers a $3.07\times$ attention speedup while preserving quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/FofGofx/sol3.

2611.32171.tldr: Shows that the frequency band in geometric RoPE variants (URoPE, RayRoPE, WorldRoPE) is an unstandardized hidden variable that can flip benchmark rankings on RealEstate10K; defines workable band ranges and traces wide-band failure to undamped depth gradients.
2611.32171.why: Directly relevant to camera-conditioned multi-view transformers and 3D-consistent video generation that use geometric RoPE; gives concrete guidance on setting frequency bands and fair comparison.
2611.32171.reason: Geometric RoPE in multi-view attention for novel view synthesis; strongly on-topic
2611.32171.qn: Careful controlled ablations and mechanistic explanation, but narrow scope and small models.
2611.32171.abs: Geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) incorporate 3D camera geometry into multi-view attention by rotating token features according to viewing rays, depths, and reprojected image coordinates. Each coordinate is rotated across a progression of frequencies--its frequency band--yet existing implementations leave this band to inherited defaults, either retaining standard 2D RoPE's top frequency or letting the frequency span grow exponentially with the attention head dimension. We show that this unstandardized setting can reverse benchmark rankings. In novel view synthesis on RealEstate10K, RayRoPE matches the strongest baseline in the 47M model (144-channel heads), yet trails by 1.2 dB in the 25M model (48-channel heads), and exhibits the same reversal when varying head size alone at fixed model width. Populating a 243x range with four frequencies instead of the 3x default at 48 channels recovers 0.9 dB of that gap. Across view synthesis and two-view depth estimation, overly narrow bands consistently blur correspondence, whereas all three projection-based encodings perform reliably when their top frequency lies within 0.3--3 rotations per 8-pixel patch (10--90 rotations across 256x256 RealEstate10K). At the opposite extreme, overly wide bands degrade RayRoPE through a forward-backward asymmetry: averaging rotations over a predicted depth interval damps high frequencies in the forward pass, yet leaves their gradients with respect to predicted depth undamped. Blocking only those high-frequency depth gradients recovers 90--93% of the lost PSNR, showing that forward smoothing does not guarantee backward stability. Guided by this analysis, we distill practical guidelines--setting bands in image coordinates, populating spans in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping--and advocate reporting and matching frequency bands in future multi-view benchmarks.

2611.32735.tldr: AnyPrune is a transformer module trained on a frozen feedforward 3DGS pipeline that scores Gaussians, picks a per-scene pruning ratio and adjusts the survivors. At 50% kept it gains 1.8 dB PSNR over the best optimization-free baseline.
2611.32735.why: Feedforward 3DGS yields millions of redundant Gaussians. A pipeline-agnostic, optimization-free pruner is directly useful for efficient feed-forward 3D reconstruction and storage.
2611.32735.reason: Pruning feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting; directly within reconstruction interests.
2611.32735.qn: Solid breadth of pipelines and views; incremental, narrow task, with zero-shot tests only on similar datasets.
2611.32735.abs: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines reconstruct a scene from images in a single forward pass, representing it as real-time-renderable 3D Gaussians. However, the resulting representations contain far more Gaussians than are needed to render the scene faithfully, especially when there are many input views. This drastically increases memory and storage requirements. Existing pruning methods either require costly re-optimization, which defeats the purpose of a single forward pass, or rely on simple strategies that do not exploit all the available information. We present AnyPrune, a transformer-based, optimization-free pruning module designed to work on top of any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. To remove unnecessary Gaussians, AnyPrune learns and exploits pipeline-specific redundancy patterns through a short single-GPU training on the frozen target feedforward pipeline. AnyPrune achieves better rendering quality than existing optimization-free pruning methods in most settings and generalizes to unseen datasets, as shown through extensive experiments across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input view counts. It prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about $5\,\mathrm{s}$ on a consumer GPU, faster than every method that merges Gaussians or re-optimizes the field. It can also be combined with the pruning built into feedforward pipelines, pruning further at moderate ratios while preserving or improving rendering quality. Finally, it can even suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that retains most of the quality.

2611.32473.tldr: OmniPersist jointly generates perspective video and a low-frame-rate panoramic stream in one video diffusion model, coupled by geometric anchoring and temporal compensation, to keep out-of-view moving objects persistent; shows gains on a new dynamic benchmark.
2611.32473.why: Directly relevant to camera-controlled video world models with 3D consistency; panoramic latent state as memory and the efficiency-motivated low-rate stream are adaptable ideas.
2611.32473.reason: Video diffusion world model with camera revisits and dynamic object persistence; strongly relevant.
2611.32473.qn: Sensible idea, but evaluated on a self-built benchmark with likely narrow baselines.
2611.32473.abs: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

2611.32998.tldr: Optimizes a 1-Lipschitz MLP SDF with sphere tracing and only multi-view patch photoconsistency, with no volume rendering, appearance model, or masks. It is initialized from classical MVS, and gets the lowest mean Chamfer on BlendedMVS and parity with leading methods on DTU.
2611.32998.why: It offers an alternative to rendering-based neural surface reconstruction, avoiding appearance-geometry ambiguity. It is relevant to optimization-based 3D reconstruction, though it is not about video or feed-forward methods.
2611.32998.reason: Neural implicit surface reconstruction from multi-view photoconsistency, a core 3D reconstruction topic
2611.32998.qn: Clean, principled idea, but depends on MVS initialization and shows only modest gains.
2611.32998.abs: Recent neural implicit and Gaussian splatting approaches have achieved impressive results in multi-view surface reconstruction. However, jointly optimizing geometry and appearance introduces ambiguities. A parametric appearance model can compensate for geometric errors, reproducing the input images accurately without an accurate surface. We demonstrate accurate neural implicit surface reconstruction using only multi-view patch photoconsistency with geometry-based visibility, without volumetric rendering or parametric appearance models. For each reference ray, sphere tracing computes the first surface intersection. Its position and normal define a local patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across visible neighboring views using colors sampled directly from the input images. For efficient sphere tracing, we use a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron. We use a single photoconsistency loss, without foreground masks or auxiliary geometric regularization. Experiments show that our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BlendedMVS (BMVS) among compared methods and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU.

2611.31757.tldr: Xtream is a streaming reconstruction pipeline that uses a 3D foundation model as a front end and a keyframe factor graph with explicit per-window metric scale, from metric 3DFM predictions or IMU. It lowers ATE on VBR, Oxford Spires and KITTI.
2611.31757.why: It addresses scale drift in feed-forward 3D reconstruction (VGGT/MASt3R-style SLAM) for long sequences, which bears directly on scalable 3D/4D reconstruction and world-model geometry.
2611.31757.reason: Large-scale streaming 3D reconstruction built on feed-forward 3D models
2611.31757.qn: Sensible, well-motivated engineering with ablations; incremental over existing 3DFM-SLAM pipelines.
2611.31757.abs: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) enable dense reconstruction in a feed-forward pass, yet their effective span is limited by cross-view attention. Local consistency has been expanded through geometric alignment of video chunks and recursive updates of an implicit memory, and large-scale scenes with pose graphs. However, both strategies are prone to drift, largely due to the lack of metric-scale observability from monocular geometry. We present Xtream,a hybrid streaming pipeline that maintains an explicit metric state through a factor graph over keyframes, while using a 3DFM as a geometric front end. Xtream incorporates metric information in two ways: through metric scale predictions from 3DFMs; or through inertial measurements if available. Across the large-scale benchmarks of VBR, Oxford Spires and KITTI, Xtream achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3DFM-based online reconstruction, reducing average absolute trajectory errors compared with published baselines and concurrent work. https://ernestolozano.github.io/xtream

2611.31892.tldr: SAMR is a training-free method for block-causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the clean KV cache and reconstructs the rest from motion-aligned history and in-flight KV. On LongLive-1.3B it cuts DiT latency 20.9% and improves late-frame PSNR 1.61 dB over token reuse.
2611.31892.why: It targets inference efficiency for autoregressive video diffusion transformers, in particular KV-cache handling for long-horizon streaming generation, which is directly relevant to your interest in efficient video DiTs and world models.
2611.31892.reason: Efficient KV cache reconstruction for streaming block-causal video diffusion, directly on core interest
2611.31892.qn: Clever, well-engineered system, but narrow scope and PSNR against dense-update outputs as proxy.
2611.31892.abs: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).

2611.32345.tldr: LRQ-Cache compresses feature caches in video DiTs using randomized SVD plus INT8 quantization, shrinking predictive cache state 42-71x (to 2.3-4.9 GiB) on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, with VBench drops up to 3.5 pp and 2.7-5.9x speedup over CPU offload.
2611.32345.why: Directly targets efficient video DiT inference: TaylorSeer/TeaCache-style caching has a memory bottleneck, and this training-free compression makes predictive caches fit on one GPU.
2611.32345.reason: Feature-cache compression for video DiTs, directly on efficient video diffusion inference
2611.32345.qn: Practical, well-motivated fix; quality drops up to 3.5 pp and the comparison baseline is CPU offload.
2611.32345.abs: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity generation, but inference is expensive because every denoising step evaluates a large transformer over all spatiotemporal tokens of the video. Temporal caching accelerates them by reusing intermediate features across denoising steps. However, retaining dense feature tensors introduces a persistent storage cost that grows with video length, resolution, and cache coverage, reaching 109-346 GiB per video for the predictive caches we evaluate. Such states exceed the memory of a single GPU, so native caches must either be offloaded to the CPU, which slows generation, or be sharded across several GPUs, e.g., with sequence parallelism, so that the cache rather than the compute sets the number of GPUs. We instead shrink the cached state itself, exploiting its redundancy: a few channel patterns shared across tokens capture much of the energy of each cached feature. Based on this observation, we propose LRQ-Cache, a training-free method that combines low-rank approximation and quantization for feature-cache compression. LRQ-Cache represents each cached feature with a small set of factors, quantizes them before storage, and reconstructs the feature at reuse time, leaving cache mechanisms unchanged. Across three caching mechanisms on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, LRQ-Cache reduces the persistent state of predictive caches by 42-71x, to 2.3-4.9 GiB per video. VBench stays within 0.25 pp of the native cache for TeaCache, and the larger drops of the Wan2.1 predictive caches, up to 3.5 pp, shrink at higher ranks. As a result, predictive caches that exceed the memory of a single 80 GB H100 GPU fit on it with LRQ-Cache, making generation 2.7-5.9x faster than with CPU-offloaded native caches.

2611.32025.tldr: Improves online 3DGS-SLAM mapping by progressively training on non-keyframes with fixed update shares, placing Gaussians via image edges, and suppressing floater opacity using a self-accumulated surface reference. Claims better appearance and geometry on egocentric and public sequences.
2611.32025.why: Relevant to optimization-based 3DGS reconstruction under real-time budgets; floater suppression and view scheduling ideas could transfer to online or feed-forward 3D pipelines.
2611.32025.reason: Online 3DGS SLAM with opacity regularization; strongly relevant to 3D reconstruction
2611.32025.qn: Sensible engineering heuristics; incremental, evidence unseen in the truncated intro.
2611.32025.abs: The realistic rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has drawn interest from real-time applications that require maps to be built online. This led to coupling 3DGS with SLAM, providing camera poses and initial Gaussians for the map. However, the map is still optimized with designs inherited from conventional SLAM, which train only on keyframes selected for localization and regularize geometry with uncertain frontend depth. These designs overlook the model complexity of a 3DGS map: with millions of parameters but few views of each region, the map overfits to sparse inputs. Resolving this is challenging, as every view and Gaussian added to the map competes for the same real-time budget. We close this gap from both sides. To add views while keyframes preserve the structure of the map, we progressively admit non-keyframe images as mapping updates complete and allocate the limited updates across different groups of frames according to the supervision each group provides. To control the model complexity of the map, edge-guided initialization places new Gaussians where image detail requires them. To complement the uncertain frontend depth, Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization (SOR) uses accumulated rendering evidence, at no extra rendering cost, to suppress the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of a map-derived surface reference. Together, these designs improve both the appearance and the geometry of online maps within the real-time budget.

2611.31689.tldr: GeoMVGen builds on a video diffusion transformer to jointly generate multi-view RGB and pointmap videos for robot manipulation. It uses modality-specific adapters, cross-modal residual links, and cross-view pointmap plus foundation-model feature-alignment losses. It reports gains over prior methods.
2611.31689.why: Joint RGB-pointmap video diffusion with multi-view consistency and action/camera control is directly relevant to 4D world models, though the components look like combinations of existing ideas.
2611.31689.reason: Multi-view video diffusion with geometry; closely matches 4D consistency interests
2611.31689.qn: Reasonable combination of known components; incremental, with evidence not visible in the intro.
2611.31689.abs: Robotic manipulation requires predicting how robot-object interactions evolve over time, encompassing both visual appearance and scene geometry. In multi-camera settings, such predictions need to capture the evolving 3D scene consistently across viewpoints, while supporting controllable generation under different robot actions and camera configurations. Existing video generation models provide strong priors for visual appearance and motion but typically lack explicit geometric modeling. Meanwhile, recent advances in geometry-aware and multi-view generation have explored joint appearance-geometry modeling and cross-view consistency, yet generating temporally coherent appearance and geometry across multiple viewpoints under robotic manipulation conditions remains challenging. In this work, we propose GeoMVGen, a framework for joint multi-view RGB and pointmap video generation in robotic manipulation. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework employs modality-specific adaptation modules to capture the distinct characteristics of appearance and geometry, while using cross-modal residual connections to facilitate information exchange between the two modalities. To establish geometric correspondences across viewpoints, we further introduce a cross-view projection mechanism with complementary geometric supervisions, combining pointmap consistency with geometry foundation model-guided feature alignment. These designs enable controllable generation of temporally evolving multi-view observations with coherent appearance and geometrically consistent scene structures. Extensive experiments on 4D video generation dataset comprising simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios demonstrate that GeoMVGen outperforms state-of-the-art methods in video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency.

2611.31478.tldr: Measures how sideways or upside-down photos (from ignored EXIF orientation tags) degrade camera pose accuracy of five feed-forward multi-view 3D models (VGGT, π3, DA3, MapAnything, VGGT-Ω) on DTU, ETH3D and Tanks and Temples; tests partial fixes.
2611.31478.why: If you use VGGT-style feed-forward reconstruction, EXIF orientation handling can silently corrupt pose results and benchmarks, including ETH3D's own sideways images. It is a practical pitfall to check.
2611.31478.reason: Rotated photos degrade feed-forward multi-view 3D foundation model pose estimation
2611.31478.qn: Useful, well-scoped diagnostic, but no new method and a limited fix analysis.
2611.31478.abs: Multi-view 3D foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D points from a set of photos in one forward pass. Many cameras store a portrait shot sideways, with an orientation tag telling viewers how to turn it, and this tag can be ignored, lost or wrong. We measure how rotated photos affect five such models on three datasets. A few rotated photos lower camera pose accuracy for every model, and the sideways photos already in a standard benchmark do the same. Even the most robust model still loses accuracy. The failure is also silent: the models' confidence does not reliably flag it, and most official image loaders ignore the tag. The fixes we test each correct only part of the problem. These findings call for orientation checks in reconstruction pipelines and benchmarks.

2611.33147.reason: Video generation of new shots from a wide view; relates to video diffusion but not 3D consistency or efficiency.
2611.33147.qn: Clear audio-grounded idea with quantified gains; benchmark is proprietary-leaning, evaluation partly described.
2611.33147.abs: Creating a dialogue scene typically requires cutting between multiple views (e.g., close-ups, medium shots, and over-the-shoulder shots) of the actors. Yet capturing such coverage is costly and in many settings unavailable. We study dialogue re-cinematography: synthesizing additional shots from a single wide-angle dialogue video. Existing video generators can synthesize new shots, but rely on visual cues alone, so when the source video barely shows the lips, the generated lip motion fails to match the speech. Our key observation is that the speech audio is view-invariant: it constrains lip motion in any target view. Building on this insight, we adapt a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model to generate the new shot from a target frame that specifies the view, a source video that contains the performance, and the speech audio that drives lip motion. In multi-person scenes, however, pretrained audio-visual models drive every visible face with the same speech, causing speech leakage, where silent listeners mouth the speaker's words. We therefore introduce speaker-aware audio gating, a training-free module that lets the audio drive only the faces that speak in the target shot. On a cinematic paired-view benchmark spanning diverse viewpoints and framings, our method lowers perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% relative to the strongest baseline, Wan 3.0. 2611.32231.tldr: ST-SfM builds a sparse 4D point cloud from synchronized calibrated multi-camera video, using temporal-median SIFT for static points and space-time interest points with HOG3D for dynamic points. It initialises 4D Gaussian splatting and beats random initialisation on three N3DV scenes.
2611.32231.why: It addresses initialisation for dynamic 4D Gaussian splatting, a core 4D reconstruction problem. The idea is relevant, but the evidence is thin and the method is classical.
2611.32231.reason: Sparse spatio-temporal SfM initialising 4D Gaussian splatting, a core interest
2611.32231.qn: Sensible classical idea, but only three scenes and compared against random initialisation only.
2611.32231.abs: Dynamic Gaussian splatting is usually initialised either with random points or with a structure-from-motion (SfM) cloud of the first frame. Neither says anything about what moves, where and when. We introduce ST-SfM, a sparse spatio-temporal SfM for synchronised, calibrated multi-camera video that splits the scene into two branches. Static structure is detected once per camera on a temporal-median image, gated for temporal stability and matched along epi-polar lines. Motion is detected as space-time interest points (STIPs) in the video volume, described with HOG3D and matched only between candidates that agree both epipolarly and in time. Union-find tracks that refuse inconsistent merges are triangulated with RANSAC over all view pairs, giving static 3D points and dynamic 4D points (x, y, z, t) with sub-frame times. We use ST-SfM derived sparse 4D cloud to initialise 4D Gaussian splatting. In comparison with random initialisation on N3DV scenes we get improvements in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS.

2611.32202.tldr: SplatTok encodes a 3DGS scene into 3D-anchored latent tokens with a transformer and decodes them into new standard Gaussians, then refines the tokens by quantization-aware latent search. It matches FCGS PSNR with 4–6.5x smaller files and beats HAC++ with 13–41% smaller files.
2611.32202.why: A feed-forward, scene-level tokenization of 3DGS with a transformer encoder and decoder bridges 3D reconstruction and latent representations, and could serve as a 3D tokenizer for generative world models.
2611.32202.reason: Learned compression of 3D Gaussian splats; strongly relevant to 3DGS
2611.32202.qn: Strong compression results across multiple benchmarks and baselines; generalization to unseen scenes shown; ablations not visible in intro.
2611.32202.abs: 3D Gaussian splats enable real-time rendering but require substantial storage. Existing compression methods either encode the primitives of a given splat or optimize a compact representation independently for each scene. Yet a Gaussian splat is only one realization of a scene: different arrangements of primitives can produce nearly identical rendered views. We exploit this freedom on the decoding side with SplatTok, a learned scene-resynthesis codec. Trained across thousands of real-world scenes, a transformer encodes an existing splat into compact, spatially anchored latent tokens, and a shared decoder synthesizes a new set of standard Gaussian primitives without preserving correspondence to the input. The representation is learned through rendering supervision rather than primitive reconstruction. At compression time, a quantization-aware latent search refines only the scene code, keeping the networks frozen, and closes most of the encoder's remaining error. On standard benchmarks, using only renders of the input splat for the latent search, without the original training images, SplatTok matches the PSNR of the feed-forward codec FCGS with 4 to 6.5 times smaller files, compressing input splats about 75 to 110 times. With the training images, it exceeds the PSNR of the per-scene method HAC++ with 13 to 41% smaller files. A single model trained on DL3DV generalizes to unseen scenes with millions of Gaussians and supports multiple target rates without retraining.

2611.31770.tldr: ET converts pretrained softmax Transformers to linear-complexity hybrid attention (exact local and shared-key softmax plus mean-anchored linear correction), calibrated gradient-free by alternating least squares. DeiT-S/B stay within 0.25 points of teachers; SD3.5-Medium matches teacher GenEval with 1.39× speedup.
